lead: This unit is about describing fluid motion, velocity, acceleration and the lines and functions that picture a flow, before any force is calculated. After it you can switch between the Lagrangian and Eulerian views, name a flow correctly, compute velocity and acceleration fields, apply the continuity equation, test a flow for rotation, and use the stream function, velocity potential, flow nets and vortex formulas.
about: Fluid kinematics describes how fluids move without asking what force causes the motion. Chapter 2.1 sets up the two viewpoints, following a particle or watching a fixed point, and the two bookkeeping devices, system and control volume. Chapter 2.2 gives names to flows and Chapter 2.3 shows the three lines used to picture them. Chapter 2.4 turns a velocity field into acceleration. Chapter 2.5 applies mass conservation to a control volume. Chapter 2.6 separates spinning flow from irrotational flow. Chapter 2.7 builds the stream function and the velocity potential, Chapter 2.8 meshes them into a flow net, and Chapter 2.9 applies the whole toolkit to swirling vortices.

chapters.idea: Fluid motion can be described by following a marked particle (Lagrangian) or by watching fixed points in space (Eulerian), and mass is tracked either as a system or as a control volume.
chapters.depth: Define the velocity field V(x, y, z, t) as a function of place and time. Lagrangian view: label each particle and give its position as a function of the label and time. Eulerian view: give the velocity at every point of space; this is the standard engineering view and the one used in all later chapters. System: a fixed collection of mass whose boundary moves with the fluid. Control volume: a fixed region of space through which mass flows, and it may be fixed, moving or deforming. Work one identification of each. Some syllabi call this pair methods of analysis or the system versus control volume approach. End with one line on choice: control volume for pipes and machines, system for following a blob of pollutant.

figure.title: Two views, two devices
figure.aria: The two description methods, Lagrangian and Eulerian, lead to the two devices, system and control volume.

chapters.example: A particle's position is x = 1 + 2t and y = 3t squared, with x and y in metres and t in seconds. Find the particle's velocity and acceleration in the Lagrangian view, then write the Eulerian velocity field and evaluate the vertical velocity at the point (3, 3). Answer: u = 2 m/s, v = 6t m/s, ay = 6 m/s squared; eliminating t gives v = 3(x - 1) m/s, so at (3, 3) the vertical velocity is 6 m/s.
chapters.trap: Writing that steady flow means no acceleration, and treating a control volume as if the mass inside it were fixed.
chapters.prereq: Unit 1: the fluid as a continuum, and the idea of a velocity field.
chapters.leave: Reynolds transport theorem, which turns system laws into control volume laws, is Unit 3.

chapters.idea: Flows are named by what does not change with time or with place, and by how orderly the motion is.
chapters.depth: Cover each pair with a plain test. Steady versus unsteady: nothing at a fixed point changes with time. Uniform versus non-uniform: nothing changes with place along the flow. One-, two- and three-dimensional flow. Laminar versus turbulent: orderly layers versus random mixing; only the definitions here. Compressible versus incompressible. Real versus ideal. Mention rotational and irrotational in one line, since Chapter 2.6 does it properly. Stress that a flow can be steady and non-uniform at the same time, as in a nozzle. Use Indian examples: steady flow from a tap set once; unsteady flow right after a power cut stops the pumps. Some syllabi list this as types of fluid flow and add 2-D and 3-D flow.

figure.aria: Four independent questions decide the name of a flow.

chapters.example: Water flows at a steady 0.02 cubic metres per second through a nozzle whose diameter falls from 100 mm to 50 mm. Find the velocity at each section and classify the flow. Answer: areas are 0.007854 and 0.0019635 square metres, so the velocities are 2.55 m/s and 10.19 m/s; the flow is steady but non-uniform.
chapters.trap: Concluding that a non-uniform flow must be unsteady, or that a steady flow has zero acceleration.
chapters.leave: Reynolds number, transition and pipe friction are Unit 4.

chapters.idea: Streamlines, pathlines and streaklines are three different drawings of the same velocity field, and they coincide only in steady flow.
chapters.depth: Streamline: the curve everywhere tangent to the instantaneous velocity, given by dx/u = dy/v = dz/w. Streamlines never cross except at a stagnation point, where the velocity is zero. Stream tube: a bundle of streamlines forming a passage. Pathline: the actual track of one particle over time. Streakline: the locus at one instant of all particles that have passed through a given point, which is what a dye filament shows. State plainly that in steady flow all three are the same curve. Note that flow lines is a general name some syllabi use for all three. Examples: smoke rising in still air is a streakline, a long exposure photograph shows pathlines.

figure.aria: The three flow lines differ by whether they show an instant, one particle, or a history of arrivals.

chapters.example: A velocity field has u = 2x and v = 3y, in m/s with x and y in metres. Find the equation of the streamline passing through the point (1, 2). Answer: dy/dx = 3y/(2x), so ln y = 1.5 ln x + constant, giving y = C x to the power 1.5; the point (1, 2) gives C = 2, so y = 2 x to the power 1.5.
chapters.trap: Assuming the pathline and the streamline are the same curve in unsteady flow, or drawing streamlines that cross.
chapters.leave: The stream function, which labels each streamline with a number, is Chapter 2.7.

chapters.idea: A fluid particle's acceleration has two parts: the change of velocity with time at a fixed point, and the change caused by the particle moving to a place where the velocity is different.
chapters.depth: Define the material derivative DV/Dt = dV/dt at fixed point plus convective part. Write all three Cartesian components, for example ax = du/dt + u du/dx + v du/dy + w du/dz, and the same shape for ay and az. Name the local (temporal) part and the convective part, and say which vanishes in steady flow and which vanishes in uniform flow. Give the convective term in streamline coordinates: V dV/ds along the streamline plus V squared over R normal to it, where R is the radius of curvature; this explains centripetal acceleration in curved flow. Some syllabi call the total derivative the substantial or Stokes derivative.

figure.title: Total acceleration
figure.aria: The local and convective parts of acceleration add to give the material derivative.

chapters.example: A flow field has u = 3x + 2t and v = 4y, with u and v in m/s, x and y in metres and t in seconds. Find the acceleration components at x = 1 m, y = 2 m at t = 1 s. Answer: u = 5 m/s and v = 8 m/s there; ax = 2 + 5 times 3 = 17 m/s squared and ay = 8 times 4 = 32 m/s squared.
chapters.trap: Using only the local term and dropping the convective terms, or confusing the field coordinates (x, y, z, t) with the path of one particle.
chapters.leave: Euler's equation and Bernoulli, which bring forces in, are Unit 3.

chapters.idea: Mass is conserved: the net mass flow out of a control volume equals the rate at which the mass inside it decreases.
chapters.depth: Derive from a small control volume. General integral form: rate of change of mass inside plus the net outflow of mass equals zero. Steady form: the sum of mass flow out equals the sum of mass flow in, written with density, area and velocity. Incompressible form: the sum of volume flow out equals the sum in. Differential form for incompressible flow: du/dx + dv/dy + dw/dz = 0, the divergence of velocity is zero. Give the two-dimensional and polar forms in one line each. Apply to a stream tube, to branching pipes and to a nozzle, and show why a gas pipeline keeps density while a water pipe does not.

figure.title: Mass balance

nodes.label: Steady, incompressible
nodes.note: sum Q in = sum Q out

figure.aria: Mass entering and leaving a control volume fixes the storage rate, and in steady flow the two flows balance.

chapters.example: A 200 mm diameter pipe carries water at 1.5 m/s. It branches into a 100 mm pipe carrying water at 1.2 m/s and a second pipe of 150 mm diameter. Find the velocity in the second branch. Answer: main flow 0.0471 cubic metres per second, first branch 0.0094, so the second branch carries 0.0377 through 0.01767 square metres, giving 2.13 m/s.
chapters.trap: Mixing up diameter and radius, and dropping density when the fluid is a gas.
chapters.leave: The full Reynolds transport theorem is Unit 3; head loss in pipes is Unit 4.

chapters.idea: Vorticity measures the spin of a fluid element, and a flow can follow curved streamlines and still be irrotational.
chapters.depth: Describe the four motions of a fluid element: translation, rotation, linear deformation and shear deformation. Define the angular velocity about the z axis as half the vorticity, and write the z component of vorticity as dv/dx minus du/dy, then the full vector as the curl of velocity. Define circulation as the line integral of velocity around a closed curve, and state Stokes theorem, that circulation equals the flux of vorticity through the enclosed area. Irrotational flow: vorticity zero everywhere, so elements translate and deform but never spin. Give a free vortex as the standard example and a forced vortex or a real pipe flow as rotational ones.

figure.title: Motion of a fluid element
figure.aria: A fluid element can translate, rotate, stretch and shear, and vorticity measures only the rotation.

chapters.example: A velocity field has u = 2y and v = minus 2x, in m/s with x and y in metres. Find the vorticity, the rate of rotation of a fluid element, and say whether the flow is rotational. Answer: the z vorticity is minus 2 minus 2 = minus 4 per second, so the element rotates at 2 rad/s clockwise and the flow is rotational.
chapters.trap: Believing that curved streamlines mean rotational flow, and forgetting the factor of two between vorticity and angular velocity.
chapters.leave: Circulation around lifting bodies and the Navier-Stokes equations go to Unit 3; vortex pressure fields to Chapter 2.9.

chapters.idea: Two scalar functions carry the two velocity components: the stream function for any two-dimensional incompressible flow, and the velocity potential only when the flow is also irrotational.
chapters.depth: Stream function: define u = dpsi/dy and v = minus dpsi/dx; it satisfies continuity automatically; units are square metres per second; psi is constant along a streamline; the difference in psi between two streamlines equals the discharge per unit depth. Velocity potential: define u = minus dphi/dx and v = minus dphi/dy, state the sign convention clearly and keep it; it exists only for irrotational flow; phi is constant on equipotential lines, which cut streamlines at right angles. Both obey Laplace's equation where the conditions hold. Say plainly that a stream function needs two-dimensional incompressible flow, so not every flow has one.

figure.title: Two functions from one field
figure.aria: One velocity field gives a stream function when the flow is incompressible and a velocity potential when it is irrotational, and their lines cross at right angles.

chapters.example: For the flow psi = x squared minus y squared, with psi in square metres per second and x, y in metres, find the velocity components, check continuity, test for irrotationality and find phi. Answer: u = minus 2y and v = minus 2x; continuity holds; vorticity is zero, so phi exists and equals 2xy.
chapters.trap: Wrong signs in u = dpsi/dy and v = minus dpsi/dx, and using a velocity potential for a rotational flow.
chapters.leave: Superposition of elementary potential flows and flow past a cylinder go to Unit 3 or beyond.

chapters.idea: A flow net is a mesh of streamlines and equipotential lines, and its geometry gives the velocity and the discharge everywhere in the field.
chapters.depth: Construction rules: streamlines and equipotentials meet at 90 degrees; the mesh cells are drawn as curvilinear squares; a solid wall is a streamline and a reservoir face is an equipotential. Discharge per unit depth between two neighbouring streamlines equals the change in psi. Velocity at a point is inversely proportional to the spacing between streamlines, so close lines mean fast flow. Uses: sketching flow past a body, flow through a sudden contraction, seepage under a dam. Some syllabi name the potential lines equipotential lines and call the whole sketch a flow net; a few ask for the number of flow channels and potential drops.

figure.title: Drawing a flow net

nodes.label: Count channels
nodes.note: q = change in psi times Nf

figure.aria: Boundaries are fixed first, then streamlines and equipotentials are adjusted until the cells are square, and the channels are counted.

chapters.example: In a flow net the stream function changes by 0.05 square metres per second between neighbouring streamlines. There are 10 flow channels between the two boundary streamlines, and 20 equipotential divisions for a total head difference of 2 m. Find the discharge per metre depth and the head drop between neighbouring equipotential lines. Answer: q = 0.05 times 10 = 0.5 square metres per second per metre depth, and each drop is 2/20 = 0.1 m.
chapters.trap: Drawing cells that are not square, and counting flow channels when the question asks for the boundary streamlines.
chapters.leave: Seepage through soil and the method of fragments belong to a groundwater or soil mechanics course.

chapters.idea: A free vortex swirls because fluid carries its angular momentum inward with no external torque, while a forced vortex rotates like a rigid body driven by an external torque.
chapters.depth: Free or irrotational vortex: tangential velocity equals a constant divided by radius; pressure rises inward; the free surface is a hyperboloid; circulation is twice pi times the constant; vorticity is zero everywhere except on the axis. Forced vortex: tangential velocity equals angular speed times radius; rigid-body rotation; the free surface is a paraboloid with rise equal to angular speed squared times radius squared over twice g; vorticity is non-zero everywhere. Give the pressure variation and the free-surface shape for both. Describe the Rankine vortex in two lines as a forced core joined to a free outer flow, and say only a few universities teach it. Examples: water draining from a tank, a stirred cup near the impeller, a cyclone separator, the casing of a centrifugal pump.

figure.aria: Free vortex velocity falls as radius grows while forced vortex velocity rises in a straight line.

chapters.example: A free vortex has v theta = 5 m/s at r = 1 m. Find the constant, the velocity at r = 2.5 m, the circulation and the surface depression at r = 1 m. Then for a forced vortex with angular speed 2 rad/s find v theta at r = 0.5 m and the surface rise there. Answer: constant = 5 square metres per second, v theta = 2 m/s at 2.5 m, circulation = 10 pi = 31.4 square metres per second, depression = 25/19.62 = 1.27 m; forced vortex gives 1 m/s and a rise of 4 times 0.25/19.62 = 0.051 m.
chapters.trap: Swapping the two velocity laws, calling a free vortex rotational, and putting r in centimetres while g is in m/s squared.
chapters.leave: Vortex flow inside pumps and turbines is applied in Units 6 and 7.
